en: Recorded with reverence:
On the tenth day of the seventh month in the eleventh year of the Hongwu era, Zongle,
abbot of Tianjie Shanshi Chan Monastery, and Ruqi, abbot of Yanfu Jiao Monastery, respectfully presented this newly annotated [text].
The *Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra*, together with officials such as Li Yong, Director of the Examination Bureau, was presented for Imperial perusal at the Xihu Lou.
On that day, an Imperial Edict was graciously received:
"This sūtra has been annotated most appropriately; it shall immediately be carved onto printing blocks and circulated, so that the monks throughout the empire may study and discuss it."
Respectfully received.
Preface to the Newly Annotated Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra:
Your Servant has heard that while the flourishing of the Dharma is said to depend upon individuals, it must also necessarily have its own appointed time.
There may be the person but not the time; there may be the time but not the person. Even if one wishes to promote [the Way], how could it be achieved?
Therefore, it must be that a ruler of brilliant wisdom and sagacity, presiding over the world during a time of peace and security, promotes it.

As for the *Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra*, our Great Awakened World-Honored One preached it two thousand years ago, and now the Emperor on High practices it two thousand years later; is this not a case of the person existing and the time being right?

Were it not so, why is it that although this scripture has flowed eastward into China for over a thousand years, none of the emperors of previous dynasties have ever devoted such profound attention and care as our Sagely Son of Heaven to investigate its essential meaning, nor issued decrees for the monastic community to study and practice it with such great flourishing?
Now, the reason our Buddha preached this sutra was to eliminate the deluded minds of sentient beings and cause them to return to the path of true reality.

Your Majesty’s intention—to have all people of the present and future worlds abandon delusion for truth and discard evil for good, thereby ascending to the realm of benevolence and longevity—is it not in perfect accord with the Buddha’s own intent?

Furthermore, the essentials of this sutra do not transcend the five dharmas, the three natures, the eight consciousnesses, and the two kinds of non-self; yet they encompass the reality and delusion, cultivation and nature, as well as the causes and effects of sages and ordinary beings—all of which are nothing other than the one mind.
Those who are able to investigate this mind will fear evil and transform toward goodness, abandon delusion and return to truth, thereby attaining the ground of self-awakened right wisdom.

Those who cannot investigate this mind will indulge their passions and give rein to their desires, flowing along until they forget their way back; they come to lose their loyalty and filial piety, ruin social customs and disturb the constant order, and willingly tread upon the path of punishment as if walking upon fire or water.
This is why our Buddha gives rise to the mind of great compassion to rescue and deliver them, just as a sovereign nurtures the common people with benevolence as if protecting an infant.

We, the monk-monks Zongle and Ruyi, yesterday received Your Majesty’s gracious edict within the inner court, wherein it was declared that the three sutras—the *Heart Sūtra*, the *Vajracchedikā*, and the *Laṅkāvatāra*—are indeed gateways for governing the mind; that the relinquishing of emotions and the detachment from attachments are fully contained therein; and that you, my subjects, must not fail to exert yourselves in this regard.

Since we, your servants, received our mandate, we have been filled with apprehension day and night, fearing we might fail to fully accord with Your Majesty’s sagacious intentions. Therefore, we have exhausted our sincerity and deliberation to provide annotated commentaries on the two scriptures, the *Heart Sūtra* and the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*, which were granted imperial approval for circulation on the twenty-eighth day of the first month in the eleventh year of the Hongwu era.

As for the *Laṅkāvatāra-sūtra*, it was only on the tenth day of the seventh month this year that its commentary could finally be completed; I have now reverently washed myself, transcribed it, and, with palms joined and head bowed to the ground, present it at the Imperial Palace.

Reflecting deeply, we, your servants, possess but mediocre talent and shallow learning; our scholarship is sparse and our understanding superficial. We truly dare not presume to join the ranks of those who provide commentaries.

Nevertheless, having received the residual grace of the rain and dew and relied upon the pure radiance of the sun and moon, we hope that our efforts may contribute even a small fraction toward the wider circulation [of this work].
Preface on the [blank] day of the seventh month in the eleventh year of Hongwu.
